newsitem.title: USA: Clinton holds double-digit leads in Ohio, Michigan.
newsitem.headline: Clinton holds double-digit leads in Ohio, Michigan.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
President Bill Clinton holds commanding double-digit leads over Republican Bob Dole in the key states of Michigan and Ohio, according to Reuters polls released on Wednesday.
Clinton also widened his lead over Dole nationally in the Reuters daily tracking poll to 11.7 percent.
The polls, conducted for Reuters by John Zogby Group International, represented more bad news for Dole, who like Clinton spent the first two days of this week campaigning in Ohio and Michigan.
These are the key findings of the polls:

-- In Michigan, Clinton leads Dole by 47.5 percent to 33 percent with 5.7 percent for Reform Party candidate Ross Perot and 9.9 percent undecided. This poll of 530 likely voters has a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points.

-- In Ohio, Clinton's margin over Dole is 47.4 percent to 35.8 percent with 5.4 percent for Perot and 11.6 percent undecided. This poll of 680 likely voters has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points.
In both states, slight majorities said Clinton deserved re-election and in both, by margins of two to one, voters said their personal finances were better than four years ago.
Significantly, in both Ohio and Michigan, nine out of 10 voters said they were not likely to change their minds before the Nov. 5 election.

Dole has narrowed the gap with Clinton in both states since the last Reuters/Zogby poll in the two states published Sept. 18, when Clinton led in Michigan by 20.5 points and in Ohio by 13.4 points. But it seems to be too little, too late with the election only 13 days away.
Both candidates have focused enormous energy and resources in the two states, which have a combined 39 votes in the Electoral College, where 270 votes are needed for election.

No Republican has ever won the presidency without carrying Ohio. But Dole's prospects seem bleak. Clinton leads among moderate voters in the state by a huge 36 percentage points. He leads by around 25 points among Catholics, who have often backed Republican candidates in the past, and he leads by almost two to one among women.

Significantly, Clinton does not seem to be exhibiting electoral coattails in either state. Asked who they would vote for in their congressional district, voters in Ohio preferred Republicans by a seven-point margin. In Michigan, voters preferred Democrats by a four-point margin.
Nationally, Clinton scored 46.2 percent against Dole's 34.5 percent. Perot polled 5.3 percent and 10.6 percent were still undecided.

The tracking Poll surveys approximately 900 likely voters over a three day period by creating a new three-day rolling average. The latest result involves the average of Sunday, Monday and Tuesday polling. The margin of sampling error is plus or minus 3.3 percentage points.
Clinton has been slowly widening his lead every day since Friday in the aftermath of the second and final presidential debate in San Diego last Wednesday.

Some Republicans are now beginning to abandon Dole and focus on the battle for Congress. The poll showed they may be having some success. Republicans have pulled slightly ahead when voters were asked their preference in their own congressional district -- 37.1 percent to 35.9 percent.
But pollster John Zogby said: "I am still operating with the '13 percent Rule' -- if Clinton's lead nationally is 13 percent or more, the Democrats have a chance of taking control of Congress."
